title: Diggers
full_review:
"Diggers" (Magnolia) is a mostly downbeat comedy-drama set in the mid-1970s, about the life and loves of Long Island clam diggers Hunt (Paul Rudd), Frankie (Ken Marino), Cons (Josh Hamilton) and Jack (Ron Eldard).

The funeral of Hunt's father, who dies alone on his boat near the film's start, is the catalyst for the younger man's reassessment of life.

As for his friends, there's the boorish Frankie, whose early scene yelling at his wife and kids while he sits on the toilet, is extremely off-putting, though Marino (who wrote the script, and comes from a generations of clam diggers) makes sure we know that despite his bark Frankie is really a loving husband and father.

Cons both deals and uses drugs. Ladies' man Jack is having an affair with Hunt's divorcee sister, Gina (Maura Tierney), which infuriates overprotective Hunt. The latter is having an affair with spoiled Manhattanite Zoey (Lauren Ambrose).

All of this plays out against the encroachment of a big fishing corporation wreaking havoc on their traditional way of life. The diggers find waters they have mined for years now off-limits to them. In one of the film's most effective scenes, Frankie decides to approach the corporation for a job and is dismissed as a nonentity.

Katherine Diekmann directs this story of the inevitability of change capably, and there are good performances all around.

Though not dull, the occasionally sordid plot is only mildly involving (more concerned with character than story development). The high quotient of expletives, however true to this particular working-class milieu, is a further detriment. Frankie has the foulest mouth of the buddies, but in addition to his basic decency he also proves to be admirably pro-life, as we observe when his beleaguered wife, Julie (Sarah Paulson), pregnant with what will be their sixth child, suggests she have an abortion and Frankie won't hear of it.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, drug and contraception references, rear male nudity, sexual encounters without overt nudity and sexual references, premarital situations, brief pornography images, domestic violence and gratuitous bathroom scenes. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
